app.title: Rømer — the first measurement of the speed of light
app.subtitle: How the eclipses of one of Jupiter's moons give you the speed of light

map.legend: The solid marker is what we see from Earth. The faint one is where the body really is right now. The gap between them is the distance the light is still crossing.

log.title: Your observations
log.empty.seen: Nothing recorded yet. Skip to the next eclipse, watch the upper row of the telescope, and press the button as the moon disappears.
log.empty.true: Nothing recorded yet. Skip to the next eclipse and watch the lower row of the telescope — that is where the moon really is.
log.notYetPlaced: Not placed yet: {count}. A timetable needs at least two observations of each kind of event before it can be worked out.
log.timetableNote: The “what your timetable says” column is not a table from somewhere else. It is your own measurement: we fit a steady rhythm through your timings and see where each observation falls away from it. Nobody has ever known when an eclipse “really” happened — the light from it is the only news there is.
solve.title: What did you get?
solve.needMore: You need at least three observations to work it out.
solve.simpleIntro: We take one eclipse from your log where Jupiter was closest and one where it was furthest. The far one arrived later, because the light had further to travel.
solve.simpleResult: Speed of light = extra distance ÷ extra time = {speed} km/s
solve.fullTitle: The careful way — all your observations
solve.fullIntro: Now let's use all your measurements instead of two. Each eclipse goes on the graph: how far Jupiter was across the bottom, and how far it fell from your own timetable up the side. The points lie on a line, and its steepness is the speed of light.
solve.comparison: The true value is {trueSpeed} km/s. You are out by {percent}%.
solve.roemer: Rømer himself got 22 minutes for the width of Earth's orbit. The right answer is 16.6 minutes — he was out by nearly a third, and still right about what mattered: light travels at a finite speed.
solve.flatResult: The speed of light cannot be worked out from this data.
solve.flatBody: The lateness does not depend on Jupiter's distance at all — the steepness of the line is indistinguishable from zero against the scatter in your own readings. That is not a bad measurement: you timed the eclipse itself, not the moment the news of it arrived.
solve.flatCompare: Switch back to “What you see” on the left, load a run of the same length, and compare the two graphs. The difference between them is Rømer's whole discovery.
solve.shortBody: Your timetable is built from your own observations. If the run does not cover about one and a half of Jupiter's cycles against Earth, then Earth is moving away (or closer) the whole time — and the steady rhythm we fit through your timings simply swallows the light delay. There is nothing left to measure. This is exactly why Rømer needed years of Cassini's records.
solve.shortSpan: Your run covers {days} days; it needs at least {needed}.
solve.meanNote: The average delay never comes out of this — the fitted timetable absorbs it. Only the change is visible. That is precisely why Rømer reported “22 minutes across the width of Earth's orbit” rather than a delay to Jupiter.
walkthrough.title: How Rømer worked it out
walkthrough.1.title: A clock in the sky
walkthrough.1.body: The moon Io goes round Jupiter once every 1.77 days, and every time it disappears into Jupiter's shadow. In the 1600s this was the most accurate clock anyone could see from anywhere on Earth, and astronomers tabulated it carefully. It was used to find longitude — on land it worked beautifully and redrew the map of Europe. At sea it never did: a telescope will not hold steady on a rolling deck.
walkthrough.2.title: Something is wrong
walkthrough.2.body: The tables said when each eclipse would happen. The observations did not match. At one time of year the eclipses came early, at another they came late — and the difference ran to a quarter of an hour.
walkthrough.3.title: The explanations that failed
walkthrough.3.body: Perhaps Io's orbit varies. Perhaps there is something odd about Jupiter. Both ideas fail on the same point: the error follows the position of the Earth. And the Earth has nothing to do with Io.
walkthrough.4.title: The idea
walkthrough.4.body: The clock is fine. What is delayed is the news. When Earth is on the far side of the Sun, the light has to cross the whole width of Earth's orbit as well — and that takes a while.
walkthrough.5.title: The prediction
walkthrough.5.body: In September 1676 Rømer announced in public that the November eclipse would arrive about ten minutes later than the tables said. It did. That is what made this science rather than a curve drawn in after the fact.
walkthrough.6.title: The number, and fifty years of doubt
walkthrough.6.body: Rømer gave 22 minutes for the width of Earth's orbit. Two years later Huygens turned that into a speed of around 200,000 km/s. Cassini, who had the same data, did not accept the conclusion — and that was not unreasonable, because the effect sat at the edge of what the timings could carry. Bradley settled it in 1728, by a completely different route.
notes.datesWarning: The eclipses in this model happen at the right rate, but not on the exact dates they happened in history. The pattern you measure is real; the dates on screen are not.
timing.seenNote: You are timing the moment the light reaches you — exactly what every real observer has ever done. The lateness will grow as Jupiter gets further away.
timing.trueNote: You are timing the eclipse itself, as if light were infinitely fast. Nobody can do this — it is the control experiment. Now Earth's position will make no difference at all.
campaign.note: Jupiter returns to the same arrangement with Earth every 399 days. The longer the run, the clearer it is that the delay comes back — which no drifting clock and no tiring observer would ever do.
clock.jumpNearest: Jump to where Jupiter is nearest
clock.jumpFurthest: Jump to where Jupiter is furthest
jovian.caption: Light from Jupiter takes {minutes} minutes. In that time {moon} moves {degrees}° round its orbit — which is why the solid and faint markers do not sit on top of each other.
curve.title: How the delay changes through the year
curve.intro: This plots how much bigger or smaller the delay is than usual — not how big it is. That is not something the method can find: the fitted timetable absorbs the average. Only the change shows, and the change is large enough: about {swing} minutes between Jupiter at its nearest and at its furthest.
curve.caption: From {from} to {to}. The upright line shows where you are now.
curve.overlay.seen: Your readings on the plot: {count}. How far each one falls from your own timetable simply is the change in the light travel time — so the points land on the curve without anything being fitted, scaled or shifted.
curve.overlay.true: Your readings on the plot: {count}. They lie flat on zero while the curve goes on swinging. When you time the eclipse itself, Earth's position makes no difference — and there is nothing to measure.
curve.overlayEmpty: Record some observations of your own and they will appear on this plot as well.
telescope.zoomHint: The moons sit close together — zoom in to separate them.
log.step1: In the controls on the left, pick a moon and click “Skip to the next eclipse” or “Watch an eclipse close up”.
log.step2.seen: Watch the upper row of the telescope — that is the view down the tube. The moon fades for about three and a half minutes before it goes.
log.step2.true: Watch the lower row of the telescope — that is where the moons really are. Here too the moon fades for about three and a half minutes.
log.step3: The moment you think it has gone, press the button below (or the space bar).
log.recorded: Recorded. Observations so far: {count}. The differences appear once there are enough to build a timetable from.
log.nothingThere: No eclipse is happening just now. Skip to the next one and wait for it.
jovian.title: Jupiter and its four moons
jovian.clock: Each of these four moons goes round Jupiter at a perfectly steady rate — Io every 1.77 days, Europa 3.55, Ganymede 7.15 and Callisto 16.69. Io and Europa vanish into Jupiter's shadow on every single orbit; the outer two sometimes slip past it. So this is a piece of clockwork that ticks at a fixed rate and can be seen from anywhere on Earth. That is exactly why it can reveal a delay in light: when an eclipse arrives at the wrong time, the fault cannot be in the clock.
comparison.title: What you see, and what is really there
comparison.intro: All three numbers below say the same one thing: the picture in your telescope is old.
comparison.seenValue: You are seeing {moon} as it looked {minutes} minutes ago.
comparison.actualValue: In that time {moon} has travelled {degrees}° round its orbit. That is where it is now.
comparison.gapLabel: How far the light must go
comparison.gapValue: {millionKm} million km from Jupiter to Earth.
comparison.yoursValue: You got {speed} km/s, which would make the delay {minutes} min.
comparison.yoursNote: That is {minutes} min away from the real delay — your whole measurement error, turned back into time.
comparison.needMeasurement: Record at least three observations and work out the speed, and your own number will appear here too.
comparison.flat: No speed comes out of this experiment — and that is precisely the point. With no delay in the news, there is nothing to measure.
game.title: An unknown universe
game.intro: In this universe light travels slower than it really does — and nobody is going to tell you by how much. Same moons, same telescope, same method. Measure it, and only then look at the answer. This is exactly where Rømer stood, minus three hundred years of hindsight.
game.notYet: Not enough yet. Gather observations covering at least two years and your number will appear here.
game.yours: Your measurements say light is {slowdown}× slower than it really is — that is {speed} km/s.
game.verdict.excellent: You are {percent}% out — better than this method can usually manage. Excellent.
game.verdict.good: You are {percent}% out. That is an honest measurement.
game.verdict.roemer: You are {percent}% out — about the same as Rømer, who was a third wrong and still right about what mattered.
game.verdict.far: You are {percent}% out. Try a longer run or more careful timings — and check whether the points on the graph really do lie on a line.
